purpose: Lanreotide is used to treat certain conditions where your body makes too much of specific hormones, such as acromegaly, which is caused by too much growth hormone. It is also used to treat certain tumors in the gut and pancreas called gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors. In some cases, it helps relieve symptoms like flushing and diarrhea caused by these tumors.
how_it_works: Your body naturally makes a hormone called somatostatin that tells certain glands to slow down hormone production. Lanreotide works like a longer-lasting copy of that natural hormone, helping to block the release of too much growth hormone or other hormones that are causing problems. By slowing down these overactive signals, lanreotide helps bring hormone levels back toward normal and can shrink or slow the growth of certain tumors.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include diarrhea, stomach pain, nausea, and loose stools. You may also notice injection site reactions like redness or discomfort where the shot is given. Some people develop gallstones, changes in blood sugar levels, or feel tired or have headaches.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you have diabetes, as lanreotide can affect your blood sugar and your diabetes medications may need to be adjusted. Because this medicine can cause gallstones, your doctor may check your gallbladder regularly with ultrasound. It may also affect your heart rate, so let your doctor know if you have any heart conditions. Do not use this medication if you are pregnant or breastfeeding without talking to your doctor first.
typical_dosing: Lanreotide is given as a deep injection under the skin, usually in the upper outer part of the buttock. The typical dose is 90 mg once every 4 weeks, but your doctor may adjust the dose to 60 mg or 120 mg depending on how you respond to treatment. A healthcare provider usually gives the injection, though in some cases patients or caregivers can be trained to do it at home.
